name: Paint the Tree
description: You are given a weighted tree consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices. Recall that a tree is a connected graph without cycles. Vertices $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ are connected by an edge with weight $$$w_i$$$. Let's define the $$$k$$$-coloring of the tree as an assignment of exactly $$$k$$$ colors to each vertex, so that each color is used no more than two times. You can assume that you have infinitely many colors available. We say that an edge is saturated in the given $$$k$$$-coloring if its endpoints share at least one color (i.e. there exists a color that is assigned to both endpoints). Let's also define the value of a $$$k$$$-coloring as the sum of weights of saturated edges. Please calculate the maximum possible value of a $$$k$$$-coloring of the given tree. You have to answer $$$q$$$ independent queries.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 5 \cdot 10^5$$$) – the number of queries. The first line of each query contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le n, k \le 5 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of vertices in the tree and the number of colors to assign to each vertex, respectively. Each of the next $$$n - 1$$$ lines describes an edge of the tree. Edge $$$i$$$ is denoted by three integers $$$u_i$$$, $$$v_i$$$ and $$$w_i$$$ ($$$1 \le u_i, v_i \le n$$$, $$$u_i \ne v_i$$$, $$$1 \le w_i \le 10^5$$$) — the labels of vertices it connects and the weight of the edge. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree. It is guaranteed that sum of all $$$n$$$ over all queries does not exceed $$$5 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each query print one integer — the maximum value of a $$$k$$$-coloring of the given tree.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1223E — Paint the Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
